https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.title: I was often called a ‘P---’ and told to ‘go home’ – but I also discovered the gentle face of England
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.subtitle: Azeem Rafiq’s testimony about racism in English cricket struck many chords with the veteran sports reporter
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.text:
The past may be a foreign country but it cannot be as brushed aside, as Azeem Rafiq has discovered. Having given harrowing testimony of the racism he has suffered he has been forced to apologise for his anti-Semitic comments made more than a decade ago. Nevertheless, Rafiq’s testimony to the DCMS still stands and struck many chords with me.
Although I am a ‘Midnight’s Child’, born just as India became free, I was not brought up to hate England, but to value its goodness. My father insisted that we had an English car which he believed was far superior to Japanese rubbish and would never fail to start in the morning. He also believed that the English had superior moral standards. One of his favourite stories was about the abdication crisis. Whatever happens, he used to say, no divorced woman will be allowed to become Queen of England. In 1961, when the Queen made her first visit to India, my mother took my sisters and me to wave to her as her motorcade passed by.
Soon after I arrived in January 1969 to study engineering at Loughborough, however, I realised my colour made me an alien. I was often called a ‘P---’ and told to ‘go home’. It was just nine months after Enoch Powell’s rivers of blood speech. Nothing had prepared me for this hard, racist face of England.
Just as Michael Vaughan is alleged to have talked to Rafiq about ‘you lot’, referring to the Asians in the team, an allegation Vaughan vehemently denies, the senior partner of the London accountancy firm where I qualified to be a chartered accountant made his views on ‘you lot of Indians’ clear on the very day he hired me. ‘I hope you will live in an area where there are not too many Indians. The trouble with Indians is that they tend to congregate together.’
My problem was that I didn’t find it easy to get away from the ‘Indian lot’. While I would have very friendly telephone conversations with landladies about renting flats, the moment I rang the doorbell and they saw me, they would invariably say, ‘I am sorry, I have just let the flat.’ After many such rejections, I decided to warn them on the telephone that I was from India. One day I saw an attractive advertisement about a place in Hampstead. After the landlady said she would be delighted for me to come over, I said, ‘Oh, by the way, I am an Indian.’ For a few seconds there was silence and then she said, ‘I am dreadfully sorry, but my husband would not like that.’
Over time, many friendly white people reached out to me and I discovered that the kind, sweet, gentle, face of England that I had read about in India did exist. But when I returned to London after a stay in India in the late 1970s, I found that my skin colour could also mean physical danger.
One Friday evening in 1980 I was travelling home from The Sunday Times on the Central Line when suddenly a skinhead let fly with his fist and floored me. As I scrabbled for my glasses, he got off the train with a laugh and the rest of the passengers looked away as if nothing had happened. After that, whenever I saw a skinhead, I crossed the road and, if they were in a group marching with a Union Jack, I hid in an alleyway. For several years, once it got dark, I did not take the underground, seeking instead the security of a taxi.
But London cab drivers could not protect me from racist football fans when I reported matches. This was a time of very overt racism and, on match days, the National Front sold their magazine outside the grounds shouting, ‘Get your colour supplement.’
In March 1981, coming back from a Norwich match against Arsenal, an Arsenal fan chased me down the train shouting, ‘Coon, coon, hit the coon over the head with a baseball bat.’ It was then a popular football song. Fortunately, just as he caught up with me, I reached the first-class carriage where there was a policeman – a black woman.
Six months later, returning from reporting a match between Nottingham Forest and Leeds, I felt I would not live to see another day.
First, young boys, no more than 12 years old, taunted me. One of them pressed his face against the door of my compartment, flattening his nose against the glass in a racial ridicule. Another shouted Sieg Heil and started marching up and down the corridor. Then they entered the compartment. One of them asked me what I did. I told him I was a sports reporter. He retorted, ‘How do you know anything about football? P---s don't know anything about football, do they? Who do you work for?’
‘Sunday Times,’ I said.
‘What's your name?’ asked another boy. When I told him he said, ‘What? Not Patel? All you P---s are called Patel. That is what the P--- who owns the corner shop is called. What do you think of the National Front?’ When I made no response he asked, ‘What do you think of Enoch Powell?’
‘I understand he is a very fine Greek scholar.’ This reply seemed to throw them and for a few minutes silence reigned. Then they warned me that Chelsea supporters on the train were planning to attack me.
Sure enough they came. They roughed me up but they could not decide who should be the first to work over ‘the wog’. By the time they made their minds up the train drew near St Pancras. Suddenly the cry went up: ‘Old Bill's coming.’ The Transport Police boarded the train and the fans fled. This did much to restore my faith in this country.
But for five years after that I did not take a train, choosing to drive to football matches instead. I always arrived very early, often even before the stewards, so that I could park as near as possible to the ground. The best moment of the match was getting into my car and driving away knowing I could no longer be attacked. I also offered lifts to my white colleagues, hoping the presence of a white person next to me would provide more protection.
The press box then was uniformly white; indeed I hardly saw a non-white face in a football ground. At post-match press conferences, football managers would look hard at me as if wondering what a person of colour was doing there. It was a common belief then that Asians could not know anything about football. The popular joke was that if the Asians got a corner, they built a corner shop.
Such remarks would have been unthinkable in the cricket press boxes of this country. Unlike football many of the journalists had old Raj ties, been to India and knew Indian cricket. Also, unlike now, when cricket at the county level is more uniformly white, English cricket was remarkably multi-racial with the great and the good of the game coming to hone their skills and advertise their ability. In Somerset Ian Botham’s greatest friend was Viv Richards and there was much talk in the press box about Imran Khan’s latest white girlfriend.
The racial divide was whether England should resume playing cricket with apartheid South Africa. I spent many an evening travelling up and down the country debating with cricket followers why the ban on playing with apartheid South Africa should not be lifted. I was opposed by many cricket correspondents and administrators for whom the whites of South Africa were “kith and kin” and whose hospitality they had enjoyed when visiting the country.
It was in pursuance of this story that I had my most memorable moment in journalism, a Sunday morning coffee with Nelson Mandela at his home in Soweto in June 1991. Mandela explained how he would use sport to reach out to the Afrikaners to create his rainbow nation which he did.
And whatever racism existed, it did not ruin my dream of becoming a writer. The only job I ever got in India was through sheer nepotism thanks to my brother-in-law who was the senior partner of the country’s leading accountancy firm. When I tried for a broadcasting gig, the man who then ran sport at All India Radio asked me to get perfumes for his wife from Harrods.
In contrast, doors opened in this country from the Sunday Times, Daily Telegraph, where I worked for 12 happy years, to the BBC, without anyone ever asking me for a gift. Such bribery is unthinkable in this country.
I treasure the gentle English face where everyone always says ‘sorry’ and has a deeply ingrained sense of justice. I voluntarily chose to live here, sacrificing greater wealth in India as a chartered accountant, to become a writer. But for my daughter’s generation it is different. As my daughter puts it, “This is our home. We don’t have another home. We should be treated like everybody else.”
The challenge posed by the testimony given to the DCMS is how English cricket and society measures up to their expectations.
Mihir Bose’s Dreaming the Impossible: Creating a Non-Racial Sports World will be published next year by Birlinn.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.title: I should never have been born, says showjumper with spina bifida as she sues GP
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.subtitle: Evie Toombes, 20, is claiming millions in damages over an alleged failure to advise her mother to take vital supplements before pregnancy
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/11.text:
A showjumper with spina bifida has sued her mother’s GP for millions in damages, claiming she should have never been born.
Evie Toombes, from Lincolnshire, was born with the disorder in which the bones of the spine do not close properly around the spinal cord.
The 20-year-old has said she aims to compete in the Paralympics in the future despite the condition often resulting in her being connected to tubes 24 hours a day.
In a landmark High Court case, Ms Toombes is suing Dr Philip Mitchell in a “wrongful conception” damages claim over his alleged failure to advise her mother to take vital supplements before getting pregnant.
In the lawsuit, Ms Toombes claims that her mother would have put off having a baby had Dr Mitchell told her she needed to take folic acid supplements to minimise the risk of spina bifida affecting her baby.
The 20-year-old said that as a result, she never would have been born at all.
Her barrister, Susan Rodway QC, told the judge that she was suing for “having been born in a damaged state” and that she wanted millions in damages to cover the increased cost of living a disabled life.
Dr Mitchell, who was working at the Hawthorn Medical Practice in Skegness at the time, “comprehensively denies” liability and claims he gave Mrs Toombes “reasonable advice”.
Medics routinely advise prospective mothers of the benefits of taking folic acid supplements before conceiving and throughout the first 12 weeks of their pregnancy to ward off the risk of spina bifida.
The court heard that Caroline Toombes, who is also a keen horse rider, had gone to see Dr Mitchell to discuss her plans to have her first baby in February 2001.
“This was a very precious decision to start a family, because she herself had lost her parents when she was young,” Mrs Rodway told the judge.
However, Mrs Toombes claims that despite having a discussion about folic acid during the consultation, Dr Mitchell did not tell her of its importance in preventing spina bifida.
“He told me it was not necessary,” she told the judge. “I was advised that if I had a good diet previously, I would not have to take folic acid.”
Mrs Rodway said that, had Mrs Toombes been properly advised by Dr Mitchell, she would not have gone on to conceive as quickly as she did.
She claims that Mrs Toombes would have paused her pregnancy plans, started a course of folic acid treatment and then attempted to conceive.
“It is her evidence she would have read up on it and wouldn’t have attempted to become pregnant until she was satisfied that she had protected herself as much as possible,” she said.
If she had indeed put off getting pregnant, she would have had a “normal, healthy” baby, but one who was a “genetically different person” to Evie Toombes, the QC added.
After her birth in November 2001, Evie Toombes was diagnosed with a lipomyelomeningocele, a form of neural tube defect to the spine leading to permanent disability.
Her mobility is said to be “very limited” and she will depend more and more on a wheelchair as she grows older, while she also suffers with bowel and bladder problems, the court heard.
Dr Mitchell’s lawyer told the judge that he gave “reasonable advice” about the desirability of folic acid supplements being taken prior to pregnancy.
The court heard that it was his usual practice to tell prospective parents that 400 micrograms should be taken by those preparing for pregnancy and throughout their first trimester once pregnant.
The lawyer added that the doctor would have said that if the mother had a good diet and therefore good folic acid levels anyway, supplements would be less important, but he denied saying they were not necessary.
Judgment has been reserved and will be given at a later date.
According to her own website, Ms Toombes describes her motto in life as: “Find a way, not an excuse.”
She writes: “I was born with a form of spina bifida ... but having a passion in life gives me purpose and direction.”
In 2018, she met the Duke and Duchess of Sussex when she won the Inspiration Young Person Award at a Wellchild charity event.
